title: Building a Hot Ones lineup from our local hot sauce shop
text:
I am planning a Hot Ones challenge for my partner Marco’s birthday. I needed to know which sauces I could use and how to arrange them so the experience would be as close to the real show as possible.
One way of doing it is buying the same sauces the Hot Ones team has expertly put together. But Marco is a hot sauce lover. He appreciates both the flavour and the spiciness, and while Da Bomb has given amazing laughs on the show (and earned its reputation for brutally burning everything it touches), I wanted to give Marco a list of sauces we could try and choose from for each level.

title: Building a Hot Ones lineup from our local hot sauce shop
section: Step 1: Turning a store website into a table
text:
Step 1: Turning a store website into a table
The first step was to search the catalog of our favourite hot sauce store: Lucifer’s House of Heat. We are going there this weekend to sample the candidates I am putting together. To do this, I downloaded the source HTML code of their product pages and parsed it into a table with the sauce name, vendor and price. The parsing code is in the folder for this post on GitHub.
HTML is the language web pages are written in. It has a specific grammar that tells your browser how to read the information. A great feature of this language is that every element is wrapped in an opening tag <...> and a closing tag </...>. Each tag can also carry a class, which is a label the website uses to style things. On this page, every product name sits inside a tag with the class grid-product__title, and every vendor inside grid-product__vendor. For example:
<div class="grid-product__title">Heartbeat Hot Sauce Pineapple Habanero</div>
<div class="grid-product__vendor">Heartbeat Hot Sauce</div>
If we look carefully and tune out the specifics of the grammar, there is a pattern we can exploit. Every product on the page sits inside a block with the class product-grid-item, and inside each block the name, vendor and price always live under the same labels. So we can tell a script to go block by block and pick out those three pieces.
I used Python with the Beautiful Soup library, which reads HTML and lets you search it by tag and class. A few things needed cleaning along the way:

Repeated products. The page shows the first few products twice (a featured strip above the main grid), so the script keeps track of each product’s ID and skips repeats.
Messy prices. The page writes prices as $17<sup>99</sup> so the cents look small. Read as plain text, that becomes “$17 99”. The page also hides a clean copy ($17.99) for screen readers, so the script grabs that one.
Sale prices. For sauces on sale, the “current” price is the sale price, which is what we would actually pay.




scripts/parse_sauces.py

import sys, csv, re
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

# Read the saved HTML page
soup = BeautifulSoup(open(sys.argv[1], encoding="utf-8"), "html.parser")

# Helper: get the text inside a tag and squash extra spaces
t = lambda el: re.sub(r"\s+", " ", el.get_text(" ", strip=True)) if el else ""

rows, seen = [], set()
for item in soup.select(".product-grid-item"):        # one block per product
    pid = item.get("data-product-id")
    if pid in seen:                                    # skip repeated products
        continue
    seen.add(pid)
    # Find the clean "$17.99" style price and keep the number
    m = re.findall(r"\$\d+\.\d{2}", t(item.select_one(".grid-product__price--current")))
    rows.append({"sauce_name": t(item.select_one(".grid-product__title")),
                 "price": float(m[-1][1:]) if m else "",
                 "vendor": t(item.select_one(".grid-product__vendor"))})

# Save the table
with open(sys.argv[2], "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    w = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=["sauce_name", "price", "vendor"])
    w.writeheader()
    w.writerows(rows)


To run it on a saved page: python scripts/parse_sauces.py sauces_page1.html sauces_page1.csv. I ran it on each page of the catalog and combined the results. After removing repeats, the store had 160 different sauces from 41 vendors.

title: Building a Hot Ones lineup from our local hot sauce shop
section: Step 2: How hot is each sauce?
text:
Step 2: How hot is each sauce?
To build a lineup that climbs like the show, I needed a heat rating for every sauce. Heat is measured in Scoville heat units (SHU): how many times a pepper extract has to be diluted before you can’t taste the heat anymore. A jalapeño is a few thousand SHU, a habanero is in the hundreds of thousands, and the peppers behind The Last Dab go past two million.
The store doesn’t list Scoville ratings, so I asked Claude (Anthropic’s AI assistant) to find them for me. Here is what it did, at a high level:

It searched for published ratings first. Many of these brands have been on Hot Ones, and the show publishes a rating for every sauce in each season’s lineup. That covered 73 sauces. El Yucateco publishes its own heat ranges, which covered 10 more, and a store or reviewer listing covered 2.
It estimated the rest. Most small brands simply don’t publish a Scoville number. For the remaining 73 sauces, Claude estimated a rating from the peppers in the ingredient list and from the brand’s own heat scale (for example “5 out of 10” or “mild”). Every row in the table says whether its number is published or estimated.
It grouped the sauces into five heat levels: Mild (under 5,000 SHU), Medium (5,000 to 25,000), Hot (25,000 to 100,000), Extra Hot (100,000 to 500,000) and Extreme (500,000 and up).

A word of caution: Scoville numbers are rough even when they are published. Peppers vary from batch to batch, and the same sauce has been listed with different ratings in different seasons of the show. The estimates are rougher still. Our tasting this weekend will be the real test.

Show the code for the Scoville plot
plot_df = (sauces.dropna(subset=["scoville_shu"])          # drops 2 gift packs
           .sort_values("scoville_shu", kind="stable"))

fig = px.scatter(
    plot_df, x="sauce_name", y="scoville_shu",
    color="heat_level", color_discrete_map=LEVEL_COLORS,
    category_orders={"heat_level": LEVEL_ORDER,
                     "sauce_name": plot_df["sauce_name"].tolist()},
    log_y=True, hover_name="sauce_name",
    hover_data={"sauce_name": False, "vendor": True, "scoville_shu": ":,",
                "heat_level": True, "source_type": True, "price": ":$.2f"},
    labels={"scoville_shu": "Scoville (SHU)", "heat_level": "Heat level",
            "source_type": "Source", "vendor": "Vendor", "price": "Price"},
)
fig.update_traces(marker=dict(size=9, line=dict(width=1, color="white")))
fig.update_layout(xaxis=dict(title="Sauce (sorted mild to hot)", showticklabels=False),
                  yaxis_title="Scoville heat units (log scale)",
                  legend_title_text="<b>Heat level</b>", template="plotly_white")
fig.show()


                            
                                            


The y-axis is on a log scale, which means each gridline is ten times hotter than the one below it. Without it, the ratings run from 500 to 820,000 and every sauce under about 50,000 would be squashed into a flat line at the bottom.

Matching the show’s ten wings
On the show, each wing is hotter than the one before. In Season 30 the step goes from about 1.3 times to 6 times hotter. To copy that, I took the most recent lineup (Season 30) and matched each sauce in the store to the wing whose rating is closest to its own. Because heat climbs by multiples, “closest” is measured on the log scale too. Wing 10 is The Last Dab, and nothing in the store comes close to it, so our finale will be whatever wins wing 9.


Show the code for matching sauces to wings
lineup = pd.DataFrame({
    "Wing": range(1, 10),
    "Show sauce (Season 30)": ["That's What Shishito Said", "Hot Bergine",
                               "Pickled Garlic Sriracha", "Chickpotle",
                               "Pikliz N Scorpion", "Tropical Amarillo", "8 Dragon",
                               "Hot Ones #8", "XXX Salsa Vibes"],
    "Show SHU": [2100, 7900, 18000, 32000, 54000, 69000, 102000, 135600, 820000],
})

# Leave out gift packs and clearance bottles
candidates = sauces.dropna(subset=["scoville_shu"])
candidates = candidates[~candidates["sauce_name"].str.contains("CLEARANCE|Gift Pack|3-Pack", case=False)].copy()

# Distance between each sauce and each wing, on the log scale
dist = np.abs(np.log10(candidates["scoville_shu"].to_numpy())[:, None]
              - np.log10(lineup["Show SHU"].to_numpy())[None, :])
candidates["wing"] = dist.argmin(axis=1) + 1
candidates["distance"] = dist.min(axis=1)

def closest(group, k=5):
    top = group.nsmallest(k, "distance")
    return "; ".join(f"{n} ({s:,.0f})" for n, s in zip(top["sauce_name"], top["scoville_shu"]))

summary = candidates.groupby("wing").apply(
    lambda g: pd.Series({"Candidates in store": len(g),
                         "Closest 5 (SHU)": closest(g)}),
    include_groups=False)
lineup.merge(summary, left_on="Wing", right_index=True).style.hide(axis="index").format({"Show SHU": "{:,}"})

title: Building a Hot Ones lineup from our local hot sauce shop
section: Step 3: What is driving the price?
text:
Step 3: What is driving the price?
Should we get more super spicy sauces, medium or mild? Are the vendors driving the price, or is it more expensive to make the extreme sauces? Let’s visualize it!
For this part I left out clearance bottles (their prices are discounted) and the gift packs, which leaves 150 sauces.


Show the code for the correlation
df = sauces.dropna(subset=["scoville_shu"])
df = df[~df["sauce_name"].str.contains("CLEARANCE|Gift Pack|3-Pack", case=False)].copy()
df["log_shu"] = np.log10(df["scoville_shu"])

rho = stats.spearmanr(df["scoville_shu"], df["price"])
fit = stats.linregress(df["log_shu"], df["price"])
pub = df[df["source_type"] != "Estimate"]
rho_pub = stats.spearmanr(pub["scoville_shu"], pub["price"])

print(f"Spearman correlation, all sauces:   rho = {rho.statistic:.2f} (p = {rho.pvalue:.1g}, n = {len(df)})")
print(f"Spearman correlation, published only: rho = {rho_pub.statistic:.2f} (p = {rho_pub.pvalue:.1g}, n = {len(pub)})")
print(f"Price goes up ${fit.slope:.2f} for every 10x increase in Scoville (R2 = {fit.rvalue**2:.2f})")


Spearman correlation, all sauces:   rho = 0.47 (p = 1e-09, n = 150)
Spearman correlation, published only: rho = 0.47 (p = 7e-06, n = 83)
Price goes up $3.05 for every 10x increase in Scoville (R2 = 0.24)


There is a correlation between heat and price, but it is moderate. A sauce that is ten times hotter costs about $3 more, and heat explains only about a quarter of the differences in price. I used Spearman’s correlation because it works on rankings, so the huge range of Scoville numbers doesn’t throw it off. The result is the same when I keep only the sauces with published ratings, so Claude’s estimates are not what is creating the pattern.


Show the code for the price vs Scoville plot
fig1 = px.scatter(
    df, x="scoville_shu", y="price", color="heat_level",
    color_discrete_map=LEVEL_COLORS, category_orders={"heat_level": LEVEL_ORDER},
    log_x=True, hover_name="sauce_name",
    hover_data={"vendor": True, "scoville_shu": ":,", "price": ":$.2f", "heat_level": False},
    labels={"scoville_shu": "Scoville heat units (log scale)", "price": "Price ($)",
            "heat_level": "Heat level", "vendor": "Vendor"},
)
fig1.update_traces(marker=dict(size=9, line=dict(width=1, color="white")))
line_x = np.logspace(np.log10(400), 6, 100)
fig1.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=line_x, y=fit.intercept + fit.slope * np.log10(line_x),
                          mode="lines", name="Linear fit", hoverinfo="skip",
                          line=dict(dash="dash", color="#888780")))
fig1.update_layout(yaxis_tickprefix="$", template="plotly_white",
                   legend_title_text="<b>Heat level</b>")
fig1.show()


                            
                                            


Look at the left side of the plot. Among the mild sauces alone, prices go from $4 to almost $24. Something other than heat is setting the price, and my guess was the brand.

Is it the brand?
To test this, I compared three simple models: one that predicts price from heat only, one from the brand only, and one from both.


Show the code for the brand models
def ols(X, y):
    """Least-squares fit: returns coefficients, R-squared and adjusted R-squared."""
    X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(y)), X]).astype(float)
    n, k = X.shape
    beta, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)
    rss = float(((y - X @ beta) ** 2).sum())
    tss = float(((y - y.mean()) ** 2).sum())
    return beta, 1 - rss / tss, 1 - (rss / (n - k)) / (tss / (n - 1))

y = df["price"].to_numpy()
brand = pd.get_dummies(df["vendor"], drop_first=True).to_numpy(dtype=float)
_, r2_heat, adj_heat = ols(df[["log_shu"]].to_numpy(), y)
_, r2_brand, adj_brand = ols(brand, y)
beta_both, r2_both, adj_both = ols(np.column_stack([df["log_shu"], brand]), y)

pd.DataFrame({
    "Model": ["Heat only", "Brand only", "Brand + heat"],
    "Share of price differences explained (R²)": [r2_heat, r2_brand, r2_both],
    "Adjusted R²": [adj_heat, adj_brand, adj_both],
}).style.hide(axis="index").format("{:.0%}", subset=["Share of price differences explained (R²)", "Adjusted R²"])







Model
Share of price differences explained (R²)
Adjusted R²




Heat only
24%
24%

Yes, it is mostly the brand. Knowing the brand alone explains about 90% of the price differences. Adding heat on top of the brand only brings it to 92%. One caution: 40 brands means 40 numbers to fit with 150 sauces, and the 13 brands with a single sauce get their price exactly right for free. The adjusted R² corrects for that, and brand still explains about 87%. Within the same brand a sauce that is ten times hotter costs only about $1.35 more. Many brands simply charge one price for their whole line: every Heartbeat sauce is $13.99, whether it is the mild Dill Pickle Serrano or the Scorpion.
To see which brands charge more, I calculated a brand premium: how much more or less a brand’s sauces cost, on average, than the heat-only model predicts for their heat. The heatmap shows each brand’s average price at each heat level, with the premium on the right. It includes the 27 brands with at least two sauces in the store.


Show the code for the brand heatmap
df["resid"] = df["price"] - (fit.intercept + fit.slope * df["log_shu"])
vendor_summary = (df.groupby("vendor")
                  .agg(n=("price", "size"), mean_price=("price", "mean"), premium=("resid", "mean"))
                  .query("n >= 2").sort_values("premium").reset_index())
vendor_order = vendor_summary["vendor"].tolist()

grid = (df[df["vendor"].isin(vendor_order)]
        .pivot_table(index="vendor", columns="heat_level", values="price", aggfunc="mean")
        .reindex(index=vendor_order, columns=LEVEL_ORDER))
hover = [[f"{v} · {lvl}<br>" + ("no sauces" if np.isnan(p) else f"${p:.2f}")
          for lvl, p in zip(LEVEL_ORDER, row)] for v, row in zip(grid.index, grid.to_numpy())]

fig2 = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2, column_widths=[0.6, 0.4], shared_yaxes=True,
                     horizontal_spacing=0.03,
                     subplot_titles=("Average price by heat level", "Brand premium"))
fig2.add_trace(go.Heatmap(z=grid.to_numpy(), x=LEVEL_ORDER, y=vendor_order, colorscale="Blues",
                          text=hover, hoverinfo="text", xgap=2, ygap=2,
                          colorbar=dict(title="Avg price", tickprefix="$", x=0.57)), row=1, col=1)
fig2.add_trace(go.Bar(x=vendor_summary["premium"], y=vendor_order, orientation="h",
                      showlegend=False,
                      marker_color=np.where(vendor_summary["premium"] >= 0, "#e34948", "#2a78d6"),
                      hovertext=[f"{v}<br>{'+' if p >= 0 else '−'}${abs(p):.2f} vs heat-predicted price"
                                 for v, p in zip(vendor_order, vendor_summary["premium"])],
                      hoverinfo="text"), row=1, col=2)
fig2.update_xaxes(title_text="Heat level", row=1, col=1)
fig2.update_xaxes(title_text="Brand premium ($)", tickprefix="$", row=1, col=2)
fig2.update_layout(height=750, template="plotly_white", margin=dict(l=200))
fig2.show()


                            
                                            


A few things stood out to me:

The priciest brands: Seed Ranch charges about $7 more than its heat would predict and Hot Ones about $6 more. Even the mild Hot Ones sauces cost around $20, so part of what you pay for is the show.
The cheapest brands: Valentina, El Yucateco and Marie Sharp’s cost $5 to $7 less than expected. These are big brands from Mexico and Belize that are made at a much larger scale.
The surprise: Pepper North, a small Ontario brand, makes some properly hot sauces (two of them have been on the show) and sells them for $10.50.

So to answer my own question: extreme sauces are not much more expensive to make, at least not in a way that shows up on the shelf. If we want to save money, the place to do it is by picking brands, not by skipping the hot end of the lineup.
There are a few limits to keep in mind. Bottle sizes range from 5 to 12 ounces and I didn’t have that information, so some of the “cheap brand” effect could just be bigger or smaller bottles. Many brands only have two or three sauces in the store, so their premiums are rough. And these are one store’s prices, not the whole market.

title: Building a Hot Ones lineup from our local hot sauce shop
text:
What’s next
This weekend we go to the store and taste. For each wing we’ll try a few of the candidates, pick the one with the best flavour at the right heat, and the lineup will be ready for Marco’s birthday. I’ll report back on whether he survived the last wing.

title: RNA-seq Workflow Demo: From Raw Reads to Interpretation
text:
Tools: Nextflow (DSL2), FastQC, Trimmomatic, STAR, featureCounts, MultiQC, R, DESeq2, ggplot2, conda
Code: github.com/paola-arguello/rna-seq-demo

title: RNA-seq Workflow Demo: From Raw Reads to Interpretation
text:
Opening
Scientific data is messy.
Before we interpret results, data moves through multiple steps. Each one makes assumptions, adds structure and can create patterns nobody intended.
This project shows how RNA-seq data moves through that process, and where interpretation can become uncertain.

title: RNA-seq Workflow Demo: From Raw Reads to Interpretation
text:
The Question
Why does analyzing RNA-seq data require more than just running a pipeline?

title: RNA-seq Workflow Demo: From Raw Reads to Interpretation
text:
Workflow Overview
RNA-seq analysis is often presented as a sequence of steps:
Raw data → quality control → processing → statistical analysis → interpretation
In practice, each of these steps transforms the data.

Quality control decides what data is considered usable
Alignment maps reads to a reference that may not perfectly represent the sample
Quantification reduces complex read data into gene-level summaries
Statistical analysis highlights patterns under specific assumptions

At each step, information is filtered, reshaped and interpreted.
The final results depend not only on the data itself, but on how these transformations are applied.

title: RNA-seq Workflow Demo: From Raw Reads to Interpretation
text:
What I Built
The project has two parts, and they are at different stages.
Preprocessing (written, not yet run on reads). A Nextflow DSL2 workflow with one module per step: FastQC, Trimmomatic, STAR alignment, featureCounts and MultiQC. Parameters live in params.yaml and the software environment in environment.yml. I have not run it on real FASTQ files yet.
Differential expression (run). An R script simulates a count matrix, and a second script analyses it with DESeq2 and makes the figures below. The simulation has 300 genes and 3 control and 3 treated samples. I raised the mean of 25 genes by 2.5 times in the treated samples, so I know which genes should come out as differentially expressed.
The goal is not a production-ready pipeline. It is to show how analysis decisions are structured, and how they affect interpretation.

title: RNA-seq Workflow Demo: From Raw Reads to Interpretation
text:
Outputs
All results below come from simulated counts, not a real experiment.

PCA plot



PCA of variance-stabilized counts (simulated data)


A PCA plot summarizes variation across samples.
It can reveal clustering patterns, potential batch effects or outliers.
It does not explain why samples cluster, only that they do. Here the samples separate by condition on PC1, which is the treatment effect I simulated.



Volcano plot



Volcano plot of DESeq2 results (simulated data)


A volcano plot highlights genes with large changes and strong statistical signals.
It helps prioritize candidates for further investigation.
It does not confirm biological relevance.
All the significant genes point up because the simulation only increased expression. A real experiment would usually have genes going both ways.

The full table is in the repository (results/deseq2/deseq2_results.csv).
Because the simulation tells me which genes really changed, I can check the result. DESeq2 called 20 genes significant (adjusted p < 0.05). All 20 are among the 25 I simulated as changed, so there were no false positives. It missed 5. In those genes the random draws happened to give a small observed change (log2 fold change between 0.27 and 1.06), and with 3 samples per group that is not enough to pass the threshold.

title: RNA-seq Workflow Demo: From Raw Reads to Interpretation
text:
Interpretation
Differential expression analysis identifies genes whose expression levels differ between conditions.
This is a statistical statement, not a biological conclusion.
A gene can appear statistically significant because:

the effect size is large
the variability is low
the sample size is sufficient

But statistical significance does not guarantee biological importance.
Effect size, variability and context all matter. The 5 missed genes show the other side: a real change can go undetected when the sample is small.
Patterns in data do not automatically turn into biological insight. They need interpretation.

title: RNA-seq Workflow Demo: From Raw Reads to Interpretation
text:
Where Things Go Wrong
Some errors are invisible at first glance.
A Wrong Genome Build can shift coordinates so that reads map to the wrong locations, producing results that look valid but refer to the wrong biology.
Batch Effects can introduce systematic differences between groups that are unrelated to the biological condition, creating patterns that appear meaningful but are driven by technical structure.
Filtering also changes what gets tested. In this run, DESeq2’s independent filtering gave no adjusted p-value to 198 of the 300 genes, all with mean counts below about 96. None of the 25 changed genes was filtered out here, but in real data a filtered gene is easy to mistake for a gene that showed no change.

title: RNA-seq Workflow Demo: From Raw Reads to Interpretation
text:
Connecting to Statistical Reasoning
These challenges are not unique to RNA-seq.
They reflect broader questions about uncertainty, sample size and interpretation.
See: When is a genetic association real?
Statistical results depend on how much data we have, how variable it is and how we model it.
Understanding those limits is part of interpreting any result.

title: RNA-seq Workflow Demo: From Raw Reads to Interpretation
text:
Key Concepts

Batch effect: differences driven by experimental conditions rather than biology
Sample metadata: information about how samples were collected and processed
PCA: a way to summarize variation across samples
Differential expression: statistical comparison of gene expression between groups
Normalization: adjusting counts to make samples comparable

title: RNA-seq Workflow Demo: From Raw Reads to Interpretation
text:
Limitations

The preprocessing workflow has not been run on real reads yet.
The counts are simulated, with only upregulated genes and no batch structure.
It is not a clinical-grade pipeline.

Next step: run the preprocessing on a small public dataset so both parts are connected.

title: RNA-seq Workflow Demo: From Raw Reads to Interpretation
text:
Final thoughts
Understanding data is not just about building pipelines. It is about knowing where results come from, what assumptions they carry and how easily they can be mislead.

title: When is a genetic association real?
text:
Opening
Statistical results often look precise, but their meaning depends on how we interpret uncertainty, sample size, and effect size.
This project uses a simple case-control example to show how the same kind of result can feel convincing, fragile or misleading depending on the data behind it.

title: When is a genetic association real?
text:
The Question
When can we trust that an observed difference between groups reflects a real association?

title: When is a genetic association real?
text:
What I Built
I built an interactive Shiny app that lets users explore a simplified genetic association scenario.
The app compares variant carriers between two groups:

cases
controls

Users can change the number of people in each group and the number of variant carriers observed.
The app then shows how those choices affect:

odds ratio
confidence interval
p-value
interpretation

The goal is not to replace formal statistical analysis.
The goal is to make the logic of association testing easier to see.

title: When is a genetic association real?
text:
What This Shows
An odds ratio compares how common an outcome or feature is between two groups.
A value above 1 suggests the variant is more common in cases than controls.
A value below 1 suggests the variant is less common in cases than controls.
A confidence interval shows the range of values that are compatible with the observed data under the model.
Wide intervals usually mean the estimate is uncertain.
Narrow intervals can look more stable, but they still depend on the assumptions behind the analysis.
A result can be statistically significant without being biologically meaningful.
A result can also be biologically interesting but too uncertain to support a strong claim.
Effect size and significance answer different questions.

title: When is a genetic association real?
text:
Where Interpretation Fails
Some interpretation failures happen when the result looks cleaner than the data really is.
Low counts and overinterpretation happen when a small number of observations produces a large-looking effect. The odds ratio may look dramatic, but the uncertainty can be wide.
Misleading statistical significance happens when a p-value is treated as the whole conclusion. A significant result still needs context, effect size, uncertainty and study design.

title: When is a genetic association real?
text:
Connection to Workflow
This statistical reasoning also applies to gene expression analysis.
In the RNA-seq Workflow Demo, differential expression results are not meaningful just because a table contains small adjusted p-values.
They need interpretation.
Gene expression results depend on count structure, sample metadata, normalization, model assumptions and uncertainty.
The same principle applies here: a result is not just a number. It is evidence shaped by context.

title: When is a genetic association real?
text:
Key Concepts

Odds ratio — a comparison of how common something is between two groups

Confidence interval — a range that shows uncertainty around an estimate

Sample size — the amount of data supporting the result

Uncertainty — the limits of what the data can tell us clearly

Statistical significance — a signal that the observed pattern is unlikely under a specific model

title: When is a genetic association real?
text:
Limitations
This app is intentionally simplified.

It uses a basic case-control scenario

It is not a full statistical inference pipeline

It does not include multiple testing correction

It does not account for ancestry, covariates, population structure or study design complexity

The purpose is interpretation, not exhaustive modeling.

title: When is a genetic association real?
text:
Final thoughts
Understanding statistical results is not just about calculation. It is about recognizing uncertainty and limits of evidence.

title: About
text:
The core of Lunaland
I am interested in how scientific knowledge is built, challenged, and sometimes misunderstood. My work sits at the intersection of biology, statistics, and computation, but my curiosity extends beyond any single field.
The same principles that shape genomics also shape physics, economics, and even theology: we observe, we model, we interpret, and we make decisions under uncertainty.
History shows us that some of the most powerful ideas come from crossing boundaries. Einstein relied deeply on mathematics at a time when physics resisted it. Alan Turing, a mathematician, proposed a mechanism for biological pattern formation that was ignored for decades before becoming foundational.
These stories are not exceptions, they are reminders that knowledge advances when we allow ideas to move freely between disciplines.
At the same time, science is a human process. It carries bias, incentives, and limitations. Data can mislead, pipelines can break, and results can be overinterpreted.
My work focuses on making those weak points visible and turning them into opportunities for better reasoning, better tools, and clearer communication.

Meet Luna
Also at the center of my work is Luna. She is the unofficial companion to all my projects, a patient listener during work rambles and a persistent reminder that the best thinking sometimes happens outside.

title: About
text:
How I use AI tools
I think of AI as a form of extended cognition. Some researchers argue that a web-weaving spider uses its web as part of how it thinks: it tunes the threads to pick up vibrations better and catch more prey. I see these models the same way. They take on part of the work so I can spend my attention on harder questions, and they make more ambitious projects possible. For me they also open a real path to doing independent research.
I know the common worry is that these tools will make people unnecessary, and that they take away originality, creativity and critical thinking. That concern is real. But if we only look at what AI can take from us, it gets harder to decide what role we want it to have. These tools are not going away. As Dewey from Malcolm in the Middle put it when he and his brothers finally beat their dad at basketball: “The future is now, old man.” I think the best way to have a say in how they are used, in research and elsewhere, is to use them openly. If we are transparent about how we use them, we can learn together what caveats, rules and guidelines they need.
So here is how I use them. I use AI assistants, including Claude by Anthropic, while building this site and the code behind it. They help me draft and edit text, write and review code, and check for broken links and inconsistencies.
I decide what goes on the site and I review every change before it is published. The analyses, interpretations and any mistakes are mine. Results come from code in the linked repositories, and anything based on simulated data is labelled as simulated.

title: Wrong Genome Build
text:
A workflow uses genomic coordinates, variants or annotations from one genome build while interpreting them against another.
For example, a file may contain coordinates based on GRCh37/hg19, but the analysis assumes GRCh38/hg38.
This can look harmless because the chromosome names and positions still appear valid. The problem is that the same coordinate can refer to a different genomic context depending on the reference build.

title: Wrong Genome Build
text:
A workflow uses genomic coordinates, variants or annotations from one genome build while interpreting them against another.
For example, a file may contain coordinates based on GRCh37/hg19, but the analysis assumes GRCh38/hg38.
This can look harmless because the chromosome names and positions still appear valid. The problem is that the same coordinate can refer to a different genomic context depending on the reference build.

title: Wrong Genome Build
text:
Why it happens
Genome build mismatches often happen when data are combined from multiple sources.
Common causes include:

downloading public data without checking the reference build
mixing older variant resources with newer annotations
reusing BED, GTF or VCF files from a previous project
assuming chr1 versus 1 is the main compatibility issue
losing reference build information during file transfer or preprocessing

The mistake is easy to miss because many tools will still run.

title: Wrong Genome Build
text:
What breaks
A wrong genome build can affect both technical outputs and biological interpretation.
It can lead to:

variants mapped to the wrong gene or regulatory region
incorrect overlap with promoters, enhancers or exons
missing or false-positive intersections in BEDTools-style analyses
misleading annotation of genomic bins
incorrect gene-level summaries
biological claims based on shifted genomic context

The most dangerous part is that the output may look clean. A table can have coordinates, gene names and p-values while still being built on the wrong reference assumption.

title: Wrong Genome Build
text:
How to detect it
Useful checks include:

confirm the reference build from the original data source
inspect file headers, especially VCF headers
check whether chromosome naming conventions match expected files
compare a few known loci against a genome browser
examine whether many overlaps unexpectedly disappear
check whether coordinates exceed chromosome lengths for the assumed build
document the genome build explicitly in the project README or config file

A small sanity check is often more useful than trusting that the pipeline completed.

title: Wrong Genome Build
text:
How to prevent it
Preventing this problem requires making the reference build a visible part of the workflow.
Good habits include:

store genome build information in params.yaml or another config file
keep genome FASTA, annotation and index files in clearly named folders
avoid generic names like genome.fa or annotation.gtf
include build names in file paths, for example GRCh38/
validate that FASTA, GTF, BED and VCF files belong to the same build
record reference sources and versions in documentation
avoid mixing downloaded resources unless their build compatibility is confirmed

In a reproducible workflow, the genome build should not live in someone’s memory. It should live in the project structure.

title: Wrong Genome Build
text:
Tiny demo
Imagine we are checking whether variants overlap a gene region.
library(tibble)

variants <- tibble::tribble(
  ~variant_id, ~chromosome, ~position, ~assumed_build,
  "var_001", "chr1", 1000000, "GRCh38",
  "var_002", "chr1", 2000000, "GRCh38",
  "var_003", "chr1", 3000000, "GRCh37"
)

expected_build <- "GRCh38"

variants |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    build_check = ifelse(
      assumed_build == expected_build,
      "OK",
      "Check build before interpretation"
    )
  )
This only works if every row already carries its build label. Real files usually don’t, so the build has to be checked from the file itself.
For a VCF, the header is the first place to look. The length of chromosome 1 differs between builds: 249,250,621 bp in GRCh37 and 248,956,422 bp in GRCh38.
# Print the reference line and the chr1 contig line from a VCF header
bcftools view -h sample.vcf.gz | grep -E '^##reference|^##contig=<ID=(chr)?1,'
If the contig line says length=249250621, the file is GRCh37 even if the file name says otherwise. If there are no contig lines at all, treat the build as unknown and stop until it is confirmed.

title: Batch Effects
text:
Treating technical structure in the data as biological signal.
The classic version: samples cluster cleanly, groups separate nicely, and the result looks convincing.
But the separation is driven by when, where or how the samples were processed, not by biology.

title: Batch Effects
text:
Treating technical structure in the data as biological signal.
The classic version: samples cluster cleanly, groups separate nicely, and the result looks convincing.
But the separation is driven by when, where or how the samples were processed, not by biology.

title: Batch Effects
text:
Why it happens
Most datasets are not generated under perfectly controlled conditions.
Common sources:

samples processed on different days
sequencing runs split across lanes
library prep done in batches
different technicians or centers
case and control groups handled at different times

The critical failure is not the presence of batch effects.
It is when batch and biological condition overlap.
At that point, the data cannot tell you which is which.

title: Batch Effects
text:
What breaks
Batch effects don’t just add noise. They add structure.
That structure can:

create artificial separation between groups
inflate differential expression results
hide real biological signal
make models look more confident than they should be

The dangerous part is that everything can look “clean”:

PCA plots show tight clusters

volcano plots show strong hits

models converge without warnings

But the interpretation is wrong.

title: Batch Effects
text:
How to detect it
This usually shows up during exploratory analysis.
Things that have saved me more than once:

PCA colored by both condition and batch
checking whether samples cluster by sequencing date instead of phenotype
looking at metadata early, not after modeling
counting how many batches exist per group

A simple but critical question:

If I remove the condition labels, would I still see the same clusters?

If yes, something else is driving the structure.

title: Batch Effects
text:
How to prevent it
Some problems are fixable. Some are not.
Good habits:

record batch variables in metadata (date, lane, center, prep)
balance cases and controls across batches when possible
check for confounding before modeling
include batch terms in the model only when design allows it
document limitations when batch and condition are inseparable

The uncomfortable truth:

If batch and condition are perfectly confounded, no statistical method can fully recover the biology.

At that point, interpretation needs to be cautious, not clever.

title: When is a genetic association real?
text: If a genetic variant appears more often in cases than controls, when can we say the association is real?

title: When is a genetic association real?
text: If a genetic variant appears more often in cases than controls, when can we say the association is real?

title: When is a genetic association real?
text:
2. The concept
Genetic association studies often summarize results using an odds ratio (OR).

OR > 1 → variant is more common in cases

OR < 1 → variant is less common in cases

But an odds ratio on its own is not enough.
Every estimate comes with uncertainty, typically expressed as a confidence interval (CI).
This interval reflects how much the estimate could reasonably change if we observed new data.
Interpretation lives in the relationship between:

the effect size (OR)

the uncertainty (CI)

the amount of data supporting both

title: When is a genetic association real?
text:
3. A simple example
Imagine a small study:

100 cases

100 controls

Variant carriers:

Cases: 20

Controls: 10

This produces an odds ratio greater than 1, suggesting a possible association.
Now imagine repeating the same calculation with:

a much larger dataset

or slightly different counts

The odds ratio might stay similar, but the confidence interval will shrink or expand depending on how stable the data is.
Same number, different meaning.

title: When is a genetic association real?
text:
4. What can go wrong
This is where interpretation often breaks:

Focusing on the odds ratio alone
Treating OR = 2 as strong evidence without asking how stable that estimate is
Ignoring confidence intervals
A wide interval may include 1, meaning the data is compatible with no association
Equating statistical significance with importance
Large datasets can produce very small, statistically significant effects that are not meaningful
Underestimating sample size effects
Small datasets produce unstable estimates that can shift dramatically

title: When is a genetic association real?
text:
5. Why this matters across fields
This pattern shows up everywhere.

In genomics → variant associations depend on sample size and cohort structure

In RNA-seq → differential expression depends on count variability and replication

In clinical research → treatment effects depend on both magnitude and uncertainty

In machine learning → performance estimates depend on data splits and variability

Across fields, the same idea holds:

An estimate without uncertainty is incomplete.
An estimate without enough data is unstable.

title: When is a genetic association real?
text:
6. Takeaway
A genetic association is not defined by a single number.
It requires:

an effect size (odds ratio)

an estimate of uncertainty (confidence interval)

enough data to make that estimate stable

Interpretation is not about whether a result exists.
It is about how much we can trust it.
